title: Labubu-maker Pop Mart's shares extend declines as third-quarter sales plunge
description: The LABUBU exhibition, Monsters by Monsters: Now and Then, opens at the Hotel du Grand Veneur in Paris, France, on March 7, 2026. After touring Shangh
body: The LABUBU exhibition, Monsters by Monsters: Now and Then, opens at the Hotel du Grand Veneur in Paris, France, on March 7, 2026. After touring Shanghai, Taipei, and Hong Kong, the world tour celebrating the first decade of The Monsters 10th Anniversary, from which Labubu originates, arrives in Paris. The story of Labubu, the plush toy that became a pop culture icon and fashion accessory. (Photo by Riccardo Milani / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)Riccardo Milani | Afp | Getty ImagesShares of Chinese toymaker Pop Mart, known for its popular Labubu dolls, added to their more than 30% decline so far this year, following a sharp decline in third-quarter revenue. Shares were last down under 2%, paring losses after declining more than 6% in early trading Wednesday. They have ended in the red in nine of the past 12 sessions.The company reported a 45% to 50% year-on-year drop in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to a filing.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconShares of Pop Mart on 28 Oct. The steep sales decline raises questions about whether the frenzy surrounding Labubu and other collectible toys can sustain the company's rapid growth, particularly in overseas markets.The decline was particularly steep overseas, with revenue in the Americas plunging 70% to 75%, while Asia-Pacific sales dropped 65% to 70%. Revenue in mainland China fell 25% to 30%, while Europe and other regions recorded a 50% to 55% decline.The results were weaker than estimates of a 30% revenue decline, although broadly in line with buy-side expectations, according to Jefferies. The brokerage cut Pop Mart's earnings estimates for 2027 and 2028 by 9% to 12%, citing pressure on profitability from weaker overseas sales.Fourth-quarter revenue is expected to rise 3% from the previous quarter but remain 34% below year-earlier levels, according to Jefferies.Pop Mart is continuing its global store expansion, with a greater focus on flagship locations in cities including New York, Milan and Paris, while diversifying its portfolio of intellectual properties beyond Labubu, with SKULLPANDA, Hirono and Twinkle Twinkle gaining traction in overseas markets, according to Jefferies.

schema.headline: Labubu-maker Pop Mart's shares extend declines as third-quarter sales plunge

title: Trump says Iran war will end 'when I want it to' as costs reportedly balloon to $47 billion
description: US President Donald Trump speaks to the media before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on Oct. 27, 2026. Kent Nishimura | AFP | G
body: US President Donald Trump speaks to the media before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on Oct. 27, 2026. Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty ImagesU.S. President Donald Trump has reiterated his claim that the Iran war will end "whenever I want it to," but insists that Tehran cannot have a nuclear weapon.Speaking at a rally in Lubbock, Texas, Trump said "Somebody asked me before, 'When will the war in Iran end?' I said, 'Whenever I want it to end.'"Trump said it "would be very quick, but we have to have an end properly," with a "total statement" that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon.His statement comes as the President grapples with poll numbers that are near a record low due to rising energy costs and affordability issues as the U.S. heads into the midterm elections on Nov. 3.Currently, Trump's approval ratings stand at 32%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll on Monday.  Mark Zandi, Moody's Analytics' Chief Economist said on Oct. 12 that the war was costing American families an average of $2,000 so far, where $1,100 comes from higher energy costs, $540 from higher interest rate costs, and $360 due to increased military spending.The Iran conflict shows no sign of winding down, with Trump saying that he will soon decide whether to "make a deal" with Iran or "finish it off."Earlier in the month, the U.S. had evacuated diplomats from Saudi Arabia, as the New York Times reported that U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for a "short but intensive" operation for strikes  on Iran after the midterm elections. An estimate by U.S. Central Command on Oct. 16, according to a report by The Hill, also revealed that the cost of the Iran war has ballooned to $47 billion, about $3 billion more than the previous numbers. The bulk of the costs was reportedly for munitions replacements at $29 million. Washington's conflict with Iran has caused "shortfalls" in U.S. munitions, despite Trump claiming on Sept. 3 that the U.S. had  "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition.The massive price tag on the war does not include the costs of damaged military bases in the Middle East, which is estimated at $184 million as of June 29, according to a lead inspector general report to Congress. This figure counts damage to U.S. diplomatic facilities in four countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — from Iranian strikes.

schema.headline: Trump says Iran war will end 'when I want it to' as costs reportedly balloon to $47 billion

title: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for industry
description: An American flag flutters outside a Honda automobile dealership in Irvine, California, U.S., March 27, 2025. Mike Blake | ReutersDETROIT — The automot
body: An American flag flutters outside a Honda automobile dealership in Irvine, California, U.S., March 27, 2025. Mike Blake | ReutersDETROIT — The automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, an executive with Honda Motor warned Tuesday. President Donald Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal."That really would be catastrophic for the entire industry," Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor Co., said during a Reuters automotive conference in Detroit.Thomas said, ideally, the countries would also include Mexico in the arrangement and reach a trilateral deal, like the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. Trade associations representing Honda, as well as every major player in the U.S. automotive industry, have been advocating for that more comprehensive accord and against bilateral arrangements between two countries.Her comments come months after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. would not automatically extend the USMCA, moving the trade pact into an annual review process instead of a 16-year trilateral extension.Trump negotiated the USMCA to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement during his first term and it took effect in 2020. He later soured on it and accused Canada of "ripping off the United States of America for years."Thomas said she is "cautiously optimistic" that cooler heads will prevail to avoid the doubling of tariffs, which Trump threatened in August if no deal can be reached.She said she's encouraged by recent reports that the U.S. and Canada have reestablished trade talks, including easing levies on critical materials such as aluminum."Our message has been clear: We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive," Thomas said. "It's integral to our success."Honda is the second-largest producer of vehicles in Canada behind Toyota Motor, but many automotive officials have voiced concerns about the lack of a North American trade deal and tariff uncertainty due to the number of parts that regularly cross the borders for vehicle production.While Honda has established large operations in Canada, the company reports that more than 60% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. are manufactured domestically across multiple U.S. assembly plants."I never thought I would see the North American region be put at a disadvantage like this," Thomas said, adding that some overseas countries have better tariff rates.The Trump administration has negotiated trade deals with other countries such as Japan and South Korea, which are major exporters of vehicles to the U.S., that include 15% tariffs on vehicles.

schema.headline: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for industry

title: Margin debt growth slows sharply as stock market warning signs build
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City.Jeenah Moon | ReutersThe pace at which investors are borrowing money
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City.Jeenah Moon | ReutersThe pace at which investors are borrowing money to invest in stocks has cooled substantially, raising concern that the stock market may be due for a fall.Recent FINRA data shows the annual growth in margin debt fell to 31.4% in September from 53.7% in May, Bank of America technical strategist Paul Ciana pointed out in a Friday note. Ciana warned that slowing borrowing momentum from extreme levels has been associated with previous market peaks.May's growth rate in 2026 was the fourth highest since 1998, according to a BofA analysis. The three higher extremes took place in 2000, 2007 and 2021 — all of which preceded stock market declines.Earlier this year, borrowing was increasing much faster than stocks were rising. Analysts view high borrowing levels as a contrarian signal, similar to bull-bear sentiment indicators. At $1.48 trillion, margin debt in September is 1.5% below June's record of $1.5 trillion. High leverage can have snowball effects in a market downturn. Lower prices trigger demands for additional collateral or forced sales, which accelerate a downturn. Individual investors can be hit hard. Tesla investor Hy Luu, for example, refinanced his home to raise $30,000 to pay down margin debt during the stock's 2022 decline.BofA sees other market warning signs, including widening high-yield credit spreads and a rotation toward defensive sectors like healthcare and consumer staples.Paradoxically, the rotation into those sectors has pushed them to "bubble-risk levels," BofA's equity derivatives team said in a note on Tuesday. Similar shifts occurred in the late 1990s dot-com era and Covid rally, they added. "These dynamics provide further evidence that markets continue to move towards a more bubble-like state."The bull case is that the midterms could alleviate some of the market's uncertainty and trigger a relief rally, Ciana noted. "Typically, risk assets such as the S&P 500 rebound after midterms unless more severe downside risks materialize."

schema.headline: Margin debt growth slows sharply as stock market warning signs build

title: Israel election appears to have no clear winner with Netanyahu, opponent Eisenkot far short of majorities
description: TEL AVIV, ISRAEL - OCTOBER 25: Posters of former Israeli Chief of General Staff and Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot (right) and Prime Minister and L
body: TEL AVIV, ISRAEL - OCTOBER 25: Posters of former Israeli Chief of General Staff and Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot (right) and Prime Minister and Likud Party leader Benjamin Netanyahu (left) are seen as election campaigns intensify two days before the vote as campaign posters of candidates are displayed on billboards and buildings across the streets ahead of the Knesset elections scheduled for October 27, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on October 25, 2026.  Anadolu | Getty ImagesThe outcome of Israel's election hung in the balance as of Wednesday, with both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and challenger Gadi Eisenkot appearing to be well off the numbers needed to form a governing coalition.An updated Channel 13 poll early Wednesday put both blocs at 51 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, the Times of Israel reported. A coalition needs 61 to be able to govern. Channel 12 and Kan 11 showed Eisenkot's bloc slightly ahead at 52-50. Arab-led parties, which belong to neither camp, were projected at 17 to 18 seats, their strongest showing ever. Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, declared victory and said the preliminary results should give him the first right to try to form a government. "The initial exit poll results indicate a complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and his October 7 government," he said in a statement on X.  Exit polls are not the official results, which are formally published a week after the election, on Nov. ​4. Around 77.7% of eligible voters turned out to cast their ballots, the highest in a Knesset election in 27 years, according to the Central Elections Committee. The vote came as Israel's first national election since Hamas's Oct. 7, 2023 attack and the subsequent wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu's dominance of Israeli politics since 2009. Netanyahu's supporters credit him with steering Israel through the war and standing up to international pressure, while critics point to his long-running corruption trial, controversial judicial overhaul efforts, and handling of the Gaza war as evidence that he is unfit for office. Netanyahu faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over the Gaza campaign, which he has rejected. Arab party resultThe historic Arab-party result is a factor to watch in coalition talks. Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas said that "our vote will change the government." Joint List faction chairman Ahmad Tibi had previously outlined a plan to prevent Netanyahu from remaining in power after the elections, according to the Jerusalem Post.The pro-Palestinian stance of Arab-led parties aligns them more closely with Eisenkot than with Netanyahu, said Amin Saikal, an adjunct senior fellow at Singapore's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, though neither man has said he would embrace them."Even if Eisenkot's alliance wins more seats, it's less likely to be able to form a governing majority without including Arab and left-wing parties," said Michael Feller, chief strategist at Geopolitical Strategy. "The next government's policies on Iran, Palestine and security may otherwise stay the same." However, Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman, whose party is projected at seven to nine seats and is currently in the opposition bloc with Eisenkot, refused during the campaign to rely on Arab parties. Earlier on Tuesday, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners warned of strong Arab participation in the vote, drawing accusations of racism from opponents. "If we don't wake up now, we'll find ourselves with ​a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmed Tibi," he said, after a series of posts highlighting long queues at polling stations in Arab communities.  Even if Eisenkot ends up with more seats, Netanyahu may use the upcoming weeks or months to his advantage by seeking to stall the formation of the new government, said Amin Saikal, an adjunct senior fellow at Singapore's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.The prime minister will "fight for his political survival," Saikal said.

schema.headline: Israel election appears to have no clear winner with Netanyahu, opponent Eisenkot far short of majorities

title: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
description: The icebreaker Tor (right) at the port of Sabetta in the Kara Sea shoreline on the Yamal Peninsula in the Arctic circle, some 2450 km of Moscow.Kirill
body: The icebreaker Tor (right) at the port of Sabetta in the Kara Sea shoreline on the Yamal Peninsula in the Arctic circle, some 2450 km of Moscow.Kirill Kudryavtesev | AFP | Getty ImagesChina and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe.Moscow and Beijing last week have agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors, increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels. The agreement came after the EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy aimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region.Although the competing moves underscore how the once-remote region is turning into a strategic prize, analysts said that Europe's ability to challenge the emerging China-Russia partnership remains limited, given Moscow's control over the main shipping corridor and Beijing's growing commercial clout.Europe cannot realistically challenge Chinese and Russian dominance of Arctic shipping in any meaningful timeframe.Alicia Garcia-HerreroAPAC & MEA Chief Economist, Natixis CIBThat's because Moscow controls the Northern Sea Route, including shipping permits, transit fees and a vast fleet of nuclear icebreakers, while Beijing provides the cargo, vessels and industrial capacity needed to develop the corridor, she added.Europe, by contrast, has limited icebreaker capacity and Arctic infrastructure, leaving it with little leverage to challenge the partnership despite its position as a major destination market.A new geopolitical fault line?The Northern Sea Route offers itself as an increasingly attractive alternative, as Middle East disruptions expose vulnerabilities in established shipping corridors.Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO.For Moscow, the route offers an opportunity to redirect energy exports toward Asia as Western sanctions constrain its access to European markets, said industry watchers whom CNBC spoke to. On the other hand, it provides Beijing another trade artery that could reduce reliance on traditional maritime chokepoints.David Roche, a veteran strategist at Quantum Strategy & Geonomics, said the Arctic's importance lies less in its potential to transform global shipping than in the deepening economic dependence between Russia and China."The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China's control over Russia in terms of Russia's dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe," Roche highlighted.The EU has acknowledged the growing challenge, highlighting the region's strategic value in its strategy, as mentioned by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week.With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition.Kaja KallasForeign Policy Chief, European UnionCan Europe fight back?Europe isn't entirely without leverage. The EU's new strategy calls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets.It also proposes a maritime security hub and greater protection for undersea cables, reflecting growing concerns about Russian military activity and threats to critical infrastructure.Yet those strengths may not be enough to overturn the structural advantages enjoyed by Moscow and Beijing, said experts.Garcia-Herrero said Europe's leverage largely rests on its position as a major destination market and the presence of large shipping companies that have avoided the Arctic because of environmental and commercial risks.Without a sustained industrial push that the EU has only begun to discuss, Europe can raise the commercial and regulatory costs of the route, but cannot prevent or replace the China-Russia partnership that now operates it.Alicia Garcia-HerreroAPAC & MEA Chief Economist, Natixis CIBEurope also faces a strategic dilemma: engaging with the emerging corridor could deepen its reliance on Russian-controlled infrastructure, even as it seeks to reduce Moscow's economic influence.Fertmax FZCO's former global head of research, Daeijin Lee said Western operators face sanctions, insurance and compliance complications that make the route considerably less attractive than it is for Chinese companies."The Arctic gives diversification, not independence," he said.A threat to global trade?For all the geopolitical attention, the Arctic remains a marginal player in global shipping.Roche estimates Arctic trade accounts for roughly 0.3% of global shipping today and could reach about 1% by 2030.Data from Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom and CNBC calculations based on UN Trade and Development figures similarly supports the 0.3% figure, with 37.02 million tonnes of cargo transiting the Northern Sea Route in 2025 compared to the 12.72 billion tonnes of global seaborne trade in 2024.Only 3.2 million tonnes of that cargo, or less than a tenth, involved vessels transiting the entire route, rather than shipments originating or terminating in the Russian Arctic, according to the Centre for High North Logistics.But traffic may be picking up, the latest September 2026 CHNL data showed. The route recorded 104 confirmed transit voyages carrying an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of cargo by the end of September, exceeding the 3.2 million tonnes recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season.Much of the existing traffic consists of Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities rather than international container shipments.However, the route also faces significant commercial hurdles. Ice conditions restrict navigation for much of the year, while specialized vessels, insurance premiums and Russian transit fees can erode savings from shorter voyages.Matthew Wright, an analyst at Kpler, said the route remains poorly suited to replacing established shipping corridors because operators need reliable, year-round services.Lee similarly expects the Arctic to develop primarily as a seasonal express route for selected high-value cargo rather than a replacement for Suez.However, climate change could shift the balance in the long-term.A study published in the WMU Journal of Maritime Affairs projected that melting Polar ice could increase the Northern Sea Route's annual transit capacity to between 127 million and 463 million tonnes by 2050.

schema.headline: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?

title: Neil Young sues Trump committee for $10M for playing 'Rockin' in the Free World' at rally
description: Neil Young performs as part of a historic double bill with Bob Dylan at Hyde Park on July 12, 2019 in London, England. Dave J Hogan | Getty ImagesLege
body: Neil Young performs as part of a historic double bill with Bob Dylan at Hyde Park on July 12, 2019 in London, England. Dave J Hogan | Getty ImagesLegendary musician Neil Young filed a $10 million lawsuit against President Donald Trump's campaign committee for infringing Young's copyright by playing his song "Rockin' in the Free World" just before the president took the stage to speak at an Oct. 12  rally in Youngstown, Ohio.The Trump 47 Committee has caused that song, without the musician's permission, "to be played numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections," Young's lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Richmond, Virginia, alleges.Trump "was personally aware that a license would be required to play the Song at rallies," and that Young "has not, and would not, grant the required license," the suit filed Monday says.Young, 80, in 2020 sued another corporation formed by Trump, Donald J. Trump for President Inc., in Manhattan federal court for copyright infringement of "Rockin' in the Free World,"  and another song written by Young, "Devil's Sidewalk," for having played the songs without permission at campaign rallies.In that first case, Trump's corporation "asserted no defense and immediately settled shortly after it was served, promising that it would never again use 'Rockin' in the Free World' without a license and permission from Young," the new suit said.CNBC has requested comment from the Trump 47 Committee about the suit, and from Young's lawyers.The White House, when asked for comment, referred CNBC to the Republican National Committee, which did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.Young, who was born in Canada, is a naturalized U.S. citizen. He is a two-time inductee in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame: in 1995 as a solo artist, and in 1997 as a member of Buffalo Springfield. Young was also a member of the folk rock supergroup Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young.Young released "Rockin' in the Free World" in 1989.His lawsuit describes the tune as a "blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten."The lyrics include descriptions of a mother discarding her baby, addiction, and "garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity — while the repeated chorus delivers savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn't shared by all," the suit notes."In short, the Song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for," the suit says.In addition to the Trump 47 Committee, the suit lists five other defendants, identified by the pseudonym "Doe," whom Young believes are liable for infringing on Young's copyright.The Oct. 12 Trump rally that is referenced in the lawsuit was also the scene of an incident that has drawn attention from local law enforcement. Videos from the rally show several attendees apparently attacking and beating a woman, Blake Miley, who had repeatedly yelled 'fascist" at Trump while wearing a shirt bearing the message "Release the Epstein Files."Mahoning County, Ohio, Sheriff Jerry Greene reportedly is investigating three individuals in connection with the incident.

schema.headline: Neil Young sues Trump committee for $10M for playing 'Rockin' in the Free World' at rally

title: Polymarket faces renewed CFTC probe over U.S. access to offshore platform
description: Shayne Coplan, chief executive officer of Polymarket, on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 13, 2025.
body: Shayne Coplan, chief executive officer of Polymarket, on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 13, 2025. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating whether prediction market platform Polymarket violated a 2022 settlement meant to ban U.S. users from its offshore platform, according to a person familiar with the matter.The investigation is part of a broader probe the agency opened into Polymarket earlier this year, after a  Wall Street Journal expose said Polymarket paid content creators to post videos showing simulated trades and fabricated wins on dummy versions of its website. The latest inquiry focuses on whether Polymarket previously broke the 2022 settlement, and is unrelated to the platform's present operations, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly.The federal agency is inquiring into Polymarket controls that are meant to detect where customers are located, as well as the platform's advertising in the U.S., the person added.The CFTC is also looking into the company's U.S. platform that launched in late December, specifically in its customer onboarding processes and protection measures, according to the source. Reuters first reported the latest investigation.The person familiar with the inquiry did not provide a start date for when the CFTC began investigating Polymarket. News of the CFTC probe comes one week before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with polls showing Democrats leading to take control of the House of Representatives from Republicans, and a neck and neck race for the Senate, amid escalating concern from mental health experts and lawmakers about prediction markets' explosive growth in the past year. Polymarket declined to comment on the investigation. The CFTC did not respond to a request for comment. In 2022, Polymarket stopped U.S. users from accessing its platform and paid a $1.4 million civil penalty to the CFTC as part of an enforcement settlement with the agency during the Biden administration. In 2024, the CFTC opened a probe into whether Polymarket was complying with that agreement, and the Justice Department opened a related investigation. Both federal agencies closed those investigations into the platform in July 2025. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Polymarket faces renewed CFTC probe over U.S. access to offshore platform

title: Robinhood shares fall 4% as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses
description: Omar Marques | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesRobinhood shares fell 4% in after-hours trading as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earn
body: Omar Marques | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesRobinhood shares fell 4% in after-hours trading as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30,  compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 51 cents vs. 56 cents expectedRevenue: $1.42 billion vs. $1.42 billion expectedRobinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting the focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity. Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million. Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

schema.headline: Robinhood shares fall 4% as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

title: Indian investors rush to Nvidia, SpaceX, Apple as local trading apps roll out access to U.S. stocks
description: INDIA - 2026/07/22: In this photo illustration, a Spacex logo is seen displayed on a smartphone with a NYSE (New York Stock Exchange) logo in the back
body: INDIA - 2026/07/22: In this photo illustration, a Spacex logo is seen displayed on a smartphone with a NYSE (New York Stock Exchange) logo in the background.Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesMajor Indian online investment platforms are unlocking access to U.S. stocks for millions of retail investors eager to diversify into global assets as the country's markets continue to underperform.Earlier, access to U.S. markets and exchange-traded funds was limited to wealthier Indians, via global banks and wealth management firms. Groww, an Indian investment platform that accounts for more than 29% of the country's 46 million active investors across stock brokerages, rolled out the U.S. equity trading feature earlier this month, Harsh Jain, chief operating officer and co-founder of the company, told CNBC.NVIDIA, SpaceX, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Micron and Meta are the most popular companies among early users, Jain said, whose firm has provided access to more than 10,000 U.S. stocks, exchange-traded funds and fractional share ownership.Zerodha, the second-largest trading platform with a 15% share of active clients as per NSE data, has also started beta testing access to U.S. stocks and plans to launch in a few weeks, the company told CNBC.Another popular brokerage with 6.7 million active retail clients, Angel One, is also reportedly planning to launch U.S. stock trading on its platform.There is a "big interest" among Indians to invest in U.S. stocks, especially in tech companies, Nitin Jain, chief executive and director at Kotak Mahindra Asset Management Singapore, told CNBC. He added that "retail investors like whatever goes up," pointing to the frenzy among Indian investors for investing in crypto a few years back. U.S. stocks in demand"There has always been latent demand in India for investing in global companies," Somnath Mukherjee, vice president of corporate development at Zerodha, told CNBC. He said that the underperformance of the Indian stock market over the past few years and the lack of local artificial intelligence champions is driving the demand for U.S offerings. The depreciation of the Indian rupee against the dollar is also pushing investors "to keep a part of their portfolio in another currency," Mukherjee said.India's benchmark stock index, the Nifty 50, has dropped nearly 13% since the start of the year while the S&P 500 has gained over 12%. Foreign investors are fleeing the country's markets, with a record $32.5 billion in outflows in direct equities since January, as per data from Indian depository NSDL, pressuring the stock market.With the absence of any major AI company and relatively expensive valuations, investors have picked markets such as South Korea and Taiwan over India, experts said.In August, resident Indians sent over $321 million overseas for investing in equity and debt, up 111% from a year ago, according to the Indian central bank's data. In the financial year ended March 2026, outward remittances for investments in equity and debt stood at $2.6 billion.While the retail outflows are a small fraction of India's currency reserves, the worry is that they rise exactly when the rupee is weak, and US markets look strong, and thereby "amplify pressure at the worst moment," Tanvi Kanchan, associate director, head of international business and strategy, Anand Rathi Shares & Stock Brokers said.Investment now accounts for about 11.7% of total outward remittances, up from 5.8% a year ago, so Indians are shifting from spending abroad to investing abroad, Kanchan said.The exit of foreign investors and rising energy bills due to the Iran war have already hit the Indian currency, warranting the central bank to step in. Kotak's Jain cautioned that as participation increases, the Indian regulator could have "second thoughts" around allowing retail access to U.S. markets.

schema.headline: Indian investors rush to Nvidia, SpaceX, Apple as local trading apps roll out access to U.S. stocks

title: JetBlue stock surges as company outlook calms investors
description: JetBlue planes populate the tarmac on June 24, 2026 at JFK Airport in the Queens borough of New York City.  Bruce Bennett | Getty ImagesJetBlue Airway
body: JetBlue planes populate the tarmac on June 24, 2026 at JFK Airport in the Queens borough of New York City.  Bruce Bennett | Getty ImagesJetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but shares surged as the carrier's upbeat forecast that it will return to profitability appeared to calm investors after a Monday rout.JetBlue stock rose 18% in trading Tuesday after hitting a new low a day earlier as investors fretted about the company's financial future.The Monday drop came after the Wall Street Journal reported Friday that a group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners."We have no intention, no plans to file for bankruptcy. We are not engaged with any restructuring company," CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC on Tuesday. "We are focused on delivering to our shareholders what we laid out for at the beginning of our turnaround plan."She said there is a "fundamental disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results actually demonstrate."The New York airline late Monday reported that its revenue per available seat mile, a key metric measuring how much operating revenue a carrier generates for every seat flown one mile, would be up as much as 22% in the fourth quarter, bringing the annual increase to an expected 13.5% to 14.5%"We're not seeing any meaningful pushback," Geraghty said in the interview.Read more about airlines' race to win over big spendersAlaska Airlines unveils massive premium cabin overhaul in high-end travel raceBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to first-class seats and premium upgradesUnited ditches more economy seats to make room for bigger premium cabins with new layoutsCaviar and privacy: Airlines' business-class wars are hereAmerican Airlines is arriving late to the luxury travel boom. Can it catch up?First-class seats are getting so fancy they’re holding up new airplanesAirlines can’t add high-end seats fast enough as travelers treat themselves to first classJetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million. The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday."Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:Loss per share: 60 cents adjusted vs. a loss of 55 cents expectedRevenue: $2.81 billion vs. $2.82 billion expectedJetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares.JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.The airline has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals. It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines, which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines. The carrier expects to grow capacity no more than 4% in the current quarter. One bright spot, executives said, has been expanding at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport, the former home hub of Spirit, which collapsed in May.

schema.headline: JetBlue stock surges as company outlook calms investors

title: AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.
description: A drone view shows a data center at the Google Storey County Campus in the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center in Sparks, Nevada, Oct. 9, 2026.Daniel Cole |
body: A drone view shows a data center at the Google Storey County Campus in the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center in Sparks, Nevada, Oct. 9, 2026.Daniel Cole | ReutersFears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming. Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms' plans for a $95 billion stock offering, announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off. Meta's five-year credit default swaps on Oct. 27, 2026Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief."Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said. A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer.Fears 'overblown'The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets. "I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks."Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%. Amazon's five-year credit default swaps on Oct. 27, 2026Bond yields also remain elevated."It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment."Earnings in focusAlphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts. Microsoft's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending. Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to continue. Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion.S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027. More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space."Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said. CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P."It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one." Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Oct. 27, 2026.Off-balance sheet debt One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report.  "There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Monday. S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added. watch nowOracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose.Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis.  "They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers. "The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. Both of those are pointing in one direction — and that's up."Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that Oracle's investment-grade credit rating is BBB-, according to S&P. A previous version mischaracterized the company's credit rating.

schema.headline: AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.

title: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
description: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy speaks at a company event in New York on Feb. 26, 2025.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAmazon laid out its AI usage guid
body: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy speaks at a company event in New York on Feb. 26, 2025.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAmazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools.The memo, which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI.   "We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice."Under CEO Andy Jassy, Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations. Jassy has previously predicted that AI will "change the scope and speed" of day-to-day work, and potentially shrink its corporate workforce in the next few years through automation, though he's noted it will also create "other jobs." As employees rush to adopt AI tools, companies have grappled with the technology's surging costs and how to reliably measure whether the technology leads to a productivity boost or other valuable returns on investment. Companies have recently cracked down on tokenmaxxing, in which developers use AI as much as possible with little regard for output. Some companies have set limits on employees' usage of tokens, or the units of data that are processed and generated by AI models, in a bid to slow rising AI bills. Others have switched to cheaper, open-source models for certain tasks. Read more CNBC tech newsA guide to some of the biggest risks in Anthropic's IPO prospectusNvidia, AMD to invest $4 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnershipApple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phoneAnthropic's IPO plans: 900% revenue retention, but $80 billion in first-half lossesAn Amazon spokesperson said the company hasn't instituted caps on employees' token usage. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing to climb the ranks. In the memo posted Tuesday, Amazon said metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain "deeply flawed" ways of measuring teams or organizations' AI usage, adding that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity. It stopped short of telling staffers to ignore those metrics altogether, however. Token usage and code generation should be considered "with care and judgment" alongside other data, Amazon said.  "We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," the company wrote.Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, told CNBC in an interview that the company has looked to metrics such as "feature velocity" to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity.The metric looks at things like, "how many launches are we doing, how many successful changes are we making in production," he said. "Broadly, we think about this as a return on investment," Brooker said. "If there is an important problem to solve for our customers, important problem to solve for our business, we're going to invest tools, time, tokens, human effort, etc. into those." He added, "What we don't want to see is wasted effort where we are going and spending those tokens solving problems that don't matter and sometimes it's hard to know, so we do need to have some appetite for experimentation." Amazon also discouraged staffers from using AI when it doesn't make sense for a given task. "If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing," Amazon said in the memo. The company added, "An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for." watch now

title: Grand jury rejects DOJ bid to indict ex-Trump WH aide Cassidy Hutchinson: Reports
description: Cassidy Hutchinson, who was an aide to former White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows during the administration of former U.S. President Donald Trump,
body: Cassidy Hutchinson, who was an aide to former White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows during the administration of former U.S. President Donald Trump, testifies during a public hearing of the U.S. House Select Committee to investigate the January 6 Attack on the U.S. Capitol, on Capitol Hill in Washington, June 28, 2022.Evelyn Hockstein | ReutersA federal grand jury Tuesday rejected a request by the Department of Justice to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her 2022 congressional testimony about President Donald Trump's conduct during the Jan. 6, 2021, mob attack on the U.S. Capitol, The Washington Post reported.Prosecutors in the DOJ's Civil Rights Division sought to charge Hutchinson with a crime based on claims she made false statements, MS NOW said, citing two people with knowledge of the case.Hutchinson told lawmakers a second-hand account about Trump angrily lunging at a security aide after being told he could not go to the Capitol that day.Senior DOJ lawyer Neville Hedley, without naming Hutchinson in open court, on Tuesday told Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui that the grand jury in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., had rejected a requested indictment, The Post reported.It is extremely rare for a grand jury to refuse to indict when prosecutors present evidence of alleged crimes. But since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, federal prosecutors in Washington have several times failed to obtain a grand jury indictment they sought.In recent weeks, prosecutors have filed separate criminal cases in U.S. District Court in D.C. against former FBI Director James Comey and two former FBI officials with charging documents other than grand jury indictments. In both cases, the alleged conduct occurred years earlier. Typically in such cases, prosecutors would seek a grand jury indictment.Hutchinson testified in June 2022 to the House Select Committee that investigated the Jan. 6 Capitol riot by a mob of Trump supporters, whose attack delayed for hours the confirmation of Joe Biden's electoral victory in the 2020 election.She said that after Trump spoke at a rally outside the White House that preceded the attack, then-White House official Tony Ornato asked her, "Did you effing hear what happened in [the president's vehicle,] The Beast?"She testified that Ornato told her that when Trump got in the car, he was under the impression from his then-Chief of Staff Mark Meadows that they going to the Capitol, as he had claimed in his speech to supporters at the rally.When Robert Engel, the head of Trump's security detail, said the president could not go there because the area was not secure, Trump "had a very strong, a very angry response to that," Hutchinson testified that Ornato said."Tony described him as being irate," Hutchinson said, noting that Trump had said something like: "I'm the effing president, take me up to the Capitol now," according to Ornato.When Engel refused again to drive him to the Capitol, Trump "reached up towards the front of the vehicle to grab at the steering wheel. Mr. Engel grabbed his arm, said, 'Sir, you need to take your hand off the steering wheel. We're going back to the West Wing,'" Hutchinson testified.Trump "then used his free hand to lunge toward Bobby Engel," Hutchinson said she was told by Ornato. Correction: Neville Hedley is a senior DOJ lawyer. An earlier version misspelled his name.

schema.headline: Grand jury rejects DOJ bid to indict ex-Trump WH aide Cassidy Hutchinson: Reports

title: Early third-quarter earnings show a 'resilient' U.S. consumer, with signs of strain
description: A customer pushes a shopping cart with cases of Coca-Cola outside a Walmart Supercenter retail store in North Bergen, New Jersey, Nov. 21, 2025.Mike S
body: A customer pushes a shopping cart with cases of Coca-Cola outside a Walmart Supercenter retail store in North Bergen, New Jersey, Nov. 21, 2025.Mike Segar | ReutersOne word keeps appearing in third-quarter earnings reports: "resilient." That's the early read on U.S. consumers from various companies that released their results this week. Many businesses say Americans are still spending despite inflationary pressures, though not every company has enjoyed the same success.The commentary comes amid fears that diesel fuel prices, which hit an all-time high of $6.52 per gallon in September, would drive up prices on consumer products. Economists also worried that more expensive regular gas, combined with high borrowing costs and continued tension between the U.S. and Iran, would spur a pullback in consumer spending. Retail sales rose 0.8% in September, following a jump of 1.3% in August. Sales in September were boosted by rising gas station spending. Despite all those challenges, some corporate executives say the headwinds aren't yet affecting sales. "There's been a lot of noise in the market this year. There's a lot of geopolitical stuff," Royal Caribbean Chairman and CEO Jason Liberty said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday. "But I look at our business [and our results], and I think that really talks to the resilience of the business, the resilience of the consumer."Royal Caribbean reported an increase in bookings during its third quarter, while Sherwin-Williams' CEO said the quarter was evidence of the company's strength. Here's how companies are reading the consumer in the most recent three-month period: Coca-ColaThe food and beverage company beat analysts' expectations for third-quarter earnings and revenue despite what CEO Henrique Braun called an "uneven environment."Coca-Cola reported that North America unit case volume was flat, indicating demand was steady in the face of higher prices. The company's overall unit case volume was helped by higher demand outside of North America."The underlying momentum remains quite strong," Chief Financial Officer John Murphy told CNBC. "Consumer sentiment is largely unchanged in the sense that, wherever you are on the income scale, you're looking for value, and I think our system here has done a good job interpreting that."The company increased its full-year forecast and now expects its comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from a prior forecast of growth between 9% and 10%. Royal CaribbeanThe cruise company beat Wall Street's expectations for earnings per share and narrowly missed on revenue. "Our third quarter results reflect continued strong consumer demand for our vacation experiences and the accelerated momentum across our industry leading brands," CEO Liberty said in the release.The company reported that the number of guests served in the third quarter increased 9% year over year to 2.7 million vacationers and said booking volumes for 2027 were already "up in the high teens," pacing ahead of historical levels and indicating high travel demand."It's not that we don't see points of challenges, but really what we've seen is that even in those points of challenges, the consumer comes roaring back as relates to the vacation experiences," Liberty told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" following the report.Royal Caribbean shares closed up more than 5% on Tuesday.watch nowSherwin-WilliamsSherwin-Williams beat analysts' expectations for revenue but fell short of expected earnings per share.Sherwin-Williams CEO Heidi Petz said in the company's earnings release that the paint retailer's performance demonstrated "the resilience of our Company and the strength of our strategy in a challenging demand environment.""Despite muted underlying market volumes, we continued to win new customers, increase share-of-wallet and deliver sales growth across all three reportable segments," she said. Net sales increased 7.9% from the same period last year. The company attributed the gain to higher selling prices, but the benefits to profits were partially offset by increased costs of raw materials and supply-chain related expenses. And the company maintained full-year guidance, saying "customer sentiment and the leading indicators we track point to muted demand over the remainder of the year and into 2027."UPSA worker drives a United Parcel Service truck on Oct. 28, 2025, in Los Angeles, California.Mario Tama | Getty ImagesUPS beat Wall Street expectations for both earnings per share and revenue in the third quarter.Revenue in the U.S. rose 4.5% during the period to $14.86 billion. CEO Carol Tomé told investors on the company's earnings call that consumers remain "resilient" ahead of the holiday season, the company's busiest period. She said the company expects that average daily shipping volume will grow next quarter at a rate consistent with last year. However, fourth-quarter domestic average daily volume will likely fall due to reducing deliveries with Amazon, she said.UPS has been in the midst of unwinding its partnership with Amazon at the same time it's executing a broad turnaround effort to operate more leanly. The company raised its full-year forecast for the second quarter in a row, projecting consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion.Shares closed up more than 5% on Tuesday.WhirlpoolNot every company is seeing the same spending trends, however. Appliance maker Whirlpool missed on both the top and bottom lines for its third quarter and cut its full-year revenue guidance. Net sales in North America fell more than 8% year over year during the period ending on Sept. 30.Even still, the company cited its own read on "resilience." "Through disciplined working capital management, we are protecting our year end free cash flow andour balance sheet resilience to navigate challenging market conditions," CFO Roxanne Warner said in the earnings release.Shares closed up more than 3% on Tuesday.— CNBC's Amelia Lucas and Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.
